questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Amsterdam is a very international city and known for being welcoming for international students. At the same time, the anthropology department ranks number 13 in Europe, which makes it one of the best places to study anthropology. The Netherlands is only 12 hours away with flixbus, which made it easy for people to visit me. Moreover, the city reminds me a lot of Copenhagen, but just in a slightly bigger version, so it was easy to feel at home.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Amsterdam and UvA is worth it! Go there!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. The first week is an introduction week where the university provides a lot of information, and the same goes for the ESN introduction week, where you meet other Erasmus students, that are as confused as you are.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was in contact via mail with the outgoing students' office, and they respond really fast. Apart from that UvA had sent 5-6 welcome mails beforehand, which provided a lot of information. In the introduction week we got a full tour of campus, and in the introduction days we also got a tour through the city, as well as some of the other campuses.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is reaaaaally difficult to find accommodation. So the moment you know that you want to go, start searching for housing. Amsterdam has one of the biggest housing crises. I know a lot of people from KU got their housing through the lottery, but I wanted to live with my friend, so we started searching in December and eventually found something through Facebook. BUT WATCH OUT FOR SCAMMERS! I have had some interesting email correspondence with scammers... Best of luck.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I lived in a house with seven other women, who were doing internships and exchange, and it made so much sense to do. This way I got out of the uni bubble and got to know some really interesting women, I wouldn't have met otherwise. I lived in Amsterdam Zuidoost, which is quite far away from the city center, but as long as you are close to a metroline, then it is actually fine. For me it was good to also get a bit outside of the city centre, which can be really busy. I will recommend to discover the outskirts of Amsterdam as well. Each part of Amsterdam is quite different from the other.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I visited some of the students living in Prinzengracht (one of the dormitories you can get through the unviersity lottery), they seemed to have a good time in there.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: It's some time ago now, but I think it was quite easy. As far as I remember, you have to register in SIS, and also get a UvAID. They messed up my birthday so I couldn't get access in the beginning, but after some calls it got fixed. KU takes weeks to respond, the UvA only takes days...

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Mails, their website, you can call the office.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted. There was one course that I didn't get into in the first round, but after applying in the second round, I got it. So I was 10/10 successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Choose 12 credits in the first block, 12 in the second, 6 in the last- otherwise the workload will be too big.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: This is honestly the best education I've ever had. I liked the whole way of teaching and even though they are super intense at UvA (which I also heard from other studies at the UvA) you get an enormous academic gain. Expect the tripple amount of reading compared to KU. You should not go to UvA for the easy Erasmus experience. I've never studied so hard as in Amsterdam. They have three exam periods, the classes are often smaller, and it is not unusual that you are on first name basis with the lecturer. There are of course also bigger courses, where this is not the case.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had not seen that I had applied for the bachelor thesis writing course, so I ended up having to write a form of bachelor thesis. The "theme courses" in anthropology are the third year anthropology student's bachelor thesis courses. They have two of these and together they make up their bachelor thesis. So the level was really intense, but so so interesting to be a part of. And well, now I have done a trial run of writing a bachelor thesis before actually having to writing it at KU. I took a first year musicology course, and the level here was quite easy, but since it was a whole other subject, it was also challenging at times. All courses are engaging the students the whole time.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The teaching is a lot more engaging. You really have to engage with and read all the texts for the classes. In one of my courses I was asked to write a weekly reading response where I summed up all the readings from the week and made my own argument based on this (a form of mini essay). I had to hand that in every Friday at 5pm. In my other course, I had to upload extensive discussion questions for the texts every Monday before the lecture, also providing an answer to your own question, with an argument. In my two other courses, we were asked to do weekly presentations, and in the other I had to do weekly group work. So you were kept engaged through the whole course. Expect a lot of time spent on uni. People actually sit there and reads until 9pm in the evening, which also means that the campus is generally more alive. There are a lot of good study spaces (not like CSS). In my course "Worlds in transition" we never went over what the texts were about, but had to directly use them. Since we were only 12 people in the class, you had to had read the texts and truly discuss and use them.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Worlds in transition: Rethinking Life in Times of Ecological Crisis
Social Transformations in China
Introduction to Cultural Musicology
Environment & International Sustainable Development

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Worlds in Transition! Or any other course with Cristobal Bonelli. If you are interested in thinking abstract and getting your whole worldview changed, this would be a good match. It was like taking part in the Death Poets Society. 
Social transformations in China was also really interesting, and since I didn't really know anything about China, I learned a lot from it. And you also get to use your qualitative skills, by interviewing a person related to China for your essay in the end. 
Environment and International Development is a really intense four week course in January, and I really liked it.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had bought a bike when I arrived, but it did not work, so I sold it again and had to rent a swapfiets, but I can recommend renting a bike from swapfiets. It is worth.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are the same as in DK. Housing is really expensive, but that was what I expected. The technoclubs can be expensive sometimes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All kinds of stuff. Go look at CREA, they have all types of courses. Also take a look at USC, you can do all kinds of sports there. I took house dancing classes and met some of my best friends in Amsterdam. I also went bouldering and can really recommend that (they have three saunas at USC that you also get access to when bouldering. You are welcome;)).

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All the courses at CREA. You meet people who are based in Amsterdam, and in this way get a bit out of your erasmus bubble. Also go to the technoclubs or to some house events. Amsterdam is known for its house and techno scene. Go to ADE events. Check out Volkshotel, all kinds of stuff happens here. Every month the biggest flea market in Europe happens in IJ Hallen. Remember cash. Go take the free ferry to North. Go to the Ceuvel, a place where they have a lot of events and also a cute coffee that have implemented Degrowth-theory in praxis.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go see the other cities: Rotterdam, Utrecht, Den Haag. Go to all the cute Amsterdam cafes. Buy the Museumskaart! I often went to Huis Marseille and also FOAM- if you are into photography these are nice places. Go to the technoclubs: Tillatec, LOFI. And keep away from Rembrandtplein and Leidseplein. Except for Cafe de Alto, and Soceitit de Kring at Leidseplein- they are cool jazz places. There are also Bimhuis who has free jam sessions on Tuesdays. Go to Mezrab, a culture house where there is free storytelling nights on Wednesdays and Fridays. Ice skating at Jaap Eden in the Winter. Or ice skating in Museumsplein. I could keep going, but I will miss it too much if I keep writing. Just go to Amsterdam. It is really really worth it.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. It is like Copenhagen in many ways. Just more canals. And less serviceminded people in the cafes. Same weather (maybe even a bit better). No rye bread but the best bake-off section in Jumbo and Albert Heijn. If you know some German and English you are good to go; Dutch is a weird blend of this, and everyone speaks English.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Ask if they want to drink a beer or cup of coffee with you. 1-2-3 you have met a potential friend.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Sometimes they can be a bit direct. They use their ring bell loud and clear. If you bike in the wrong place you will get a curse thrown after you- oftentimes something about your grandparents and cancer in Dutch.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The imaginative spaces that seem to emerge everywhere in Amsterdam. It seems like everything could be possible in this city.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Rent a bike from Swapfiets. Take a Crea course. Go out in the city and emerge yourself in it as much as possible- you can sleep when you get back to Cph.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: It can be really hard to leave again.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Gaining academic motivation as well as getting really good friends. I thought this time would feel like a parenthesis, but I have rarely felt more alive.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Registration with the muncipality. My contract was a mess so it took me three times before I could register.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
